hypothesis: Compared with our current crisis response messaging (baseline), a structured, psychology-informed response template combined with calibrated speed/accuracy tradeoffs (treatment) will (a) improve audience trust and credibility signals (sentiment, perceived trustworthiness, willingness to wait for verification), (b) reduce harmful narrative spread (negative share-of-voice), and (c) maintain legal/compliance guardrails, when tested on synthetic or sandboxed audiences that simulate an AI-driven misinformation incident.

baseline.description: Current or typical crisis communications response used by the organization, modeled as a generic, one-off statement drafted under time pressure without explicit reference to misinformation psychology, message architecture, or predefined SLAs.
message_criteria: Single primary public statement (e.g., press release or social post) produced without a standardized template.
No explicit acknowledgment of AI-driven manipulation or deepfake risk unless already widely reported.
Limited explanation of what is known/unknown; tends to emphasize broad denial or reassurance.
No clear commitment to future updates (no explicit update cadence or SLA communicated).
Coordination with legal is ad hoc; text has only a basic compliance review with no documented checklists.
Internal and external messages may diverge in language and timing (no explicit alignment constraints).
operational_behavior: First external message is released as soon as a minimal fact-check passes (e.g., target SLA of 2–4 hours), regardless of residual uncertainty.
Internal messaging is sent either later or not fully aligned, increasing risk of leaks and inconsistent narratives.
No systematic use of influencers/partners; any amplification is organic or left to agencies without central guidance.
Impact measurement is limited to high-level media mentions and basic social engagement metrics without sentiment classification or narrative tracking.

treatment.description: A structured AI-misinformation crisis response protocol that uses pre-defined message architecture, explicit speed vs. accuracy SLAs, and coordinated internal/external communications, tested via A/B simulations on synthetic or sandbox audiences.

message_architecture: Opening that explicitly acknowledges uncertainty and AI manipulation risk where appropriate (e.g., deepfake indicators).
Clear separation of what is known, unknown, and being investigated, presented in plain, non-legalistic language.
Explicit commitment to an update cadence (e.g., initial holding statement within X minutes; full update within Y hours).
Short explanation of verification steps being taken (e.g., forensic analysis, log review, third-party validation) without disclosing sensitive operational details.
Values-anchored framing that connects actions to safety, integrity, and stakeholder protection.
Explicit guidance on what employees, customers, and partners should do or not do (calls to action or to inaction).
speed_vs_accuracy_slas: Tiered SLA matrix defined by severity and audience (e.g., internal employees vs. public vs. regulators).
Use of short holding statements that prioritize speed but are tightly scoped and clearly provisional.
Full statements only after cross-functional sign-off including legal, with target windows per severity tier.
Pre-approved phrase bank that legal has reviewed in advance, enabling rapid assembly of compliant messages.
coordination_protocol: Internal message precedes or is simultaneous with external release, using consistent core facts and framing.
Unified briefing pack for spokespeople, agencies, and key partners with aligned talking points and Q&A.
Designated approval workflow with explicit decision rights (who can green-light a holding statement vs. full update).
amplification_strategy: Pre-identified, pre-briefed influencers/partners/advocates (e.g., industry bodies, NGOs, experts) who can credibly restate or validate core messages.
Structured outreach messages tailored for partners, including shareable links, short posts, and disclaimers.
Guidelines for employees on resharing or commenting to avoid off-message escalation.
measurement_hooks: UTM parameters and trackable links in statements to support narrative and reach analysis.
Consistent hashtags and key phrases to simplify monitoring and sentiment clustering.
Pre-defined analytics notebook to ingest and visualize sentiment, reach, narrative prevalence, and click-through behavior over simulated timelines.

workloads.name: workload-1-synthetic-audience-social-feed-simulation
workloads.description: Simulated social-media environment with synthetic users exposed to an AI-driven misinformation event and then to either baseline or treatment response messages. Used to assess sentiment, trust, and narrative spread under time-pressured conditions.

misinformation_scenario.description: Synthetic deepfake video alleging the CEO made discriminatory remarks in an internal meeting, seeded across a mock social platform.

response_variants.baseline_message: Crisis statement in plain text or JSON, representing current typical practice.
response_variants.treatment_message: Templated response aligned with treatment message architecture, with placeholders filled for the scenario.

timing_parameters.treatment_response_release_time: t0 + Y minutes/hours (can be equal to X in one run, later in another to simulate tradeoffs)

steps: Generate synthetic audience with specified behavioral parameters.
Seed misinformation content at t0 and simulate engagement (views, shares, comments) for a defined pre-response period.
At configured times, inject either baseline or treatment messages into the feed for randomized user subsets (A/B assignment).
Simulate probabilistic user behaviors (view, share, like, comment, ignore, change belief) as functions of message content, trust, and timing.
Log all events (exposures, interactions, sentiment labels, belief-updates) with timestamps and user IDs.
Export event logs to the analysis notebook for metric computation.

workloads.name: workload-2-message-copy-ab-test-on-sandboxed-panel
workloads.description: Text-only A/B test of message variants evaluated by a synthetic or sandboxed panel (e.g., survey respondents, internal users, or LLM-generated proxy raters) rating trust, clarity, and likelihood to update beliefs.

questions: Likelihood you would wait for further updates before reacting
Likelihood you would share the organization’s message

steps: Randomly assign panel members to baseline or one of the treatment variants (between-subjects design).
Present standardized scenario description followed by the assigned message.
Collect numeric ratings for each question and optional free-text feedback.
Store anonymized responses in a structured table for analysis.
Run analysis to compare distributions of ratings across variants and segments.

workloads.name: workload-3-sentiment-and-narrative-shift-dashboard
workloads.description: Offline analysis pipeline and dashboard that consumes logs from Workload 1 and/or historical-like synthetic data to quantify the impact of baseline vs. treatment responses on sentiment, reach, and behavior over time.

steps: Ingest event logs into a data frame or database.
Compute time-bucketed metrics for baseline and treatment cohorts (e.g., per 15 minutes or hour).
Apply sentiment model or rule-based sentiment classifier to content and comments if not pre-computed.
Cluster content into narratives (e.g., misinformation narrative vs. corrective narrative vs. unrelated chatter).
Generate comparative visualizations for key metrics (sentiment over time, share-of-voice, engagement rate, narrative prevalence).
Export dashboard views suitable for executive review (e.g., static charts or interactive notebook cells).

randomization: Random assignment of users or panelists to baseline vs. treatment groups (and among multiple treatment variants where applicable).
Random seeding of misinformation exposure order when feasible to avoid order effects.
comparability: Ensure baseline and treatment cohorts have similar distributions across key attributes: audience segments, baseline trust levels, regions, and engagement propensity.
Use the same synthetic misinformation content across runs for all variants.
Use identical timing parameters for response release where testing the effect of message content; manipulate timing only in dedicated speed vs. accuracy sub-experiments.
blinding: Sandboxed human raters should not be informed whether a message is baseline or treatment.
Analysis notebooks should be able to run with message_variant labels masked during exploratory analysis to reduce bias (optional).
legal_and_policy_constraints: All simulated messages must be clearly marked as synthetic and must not be deployed to real, uncontrolled public channels without legal and ethics review.
When using internal employees as raters, ensure participation is voluntary and data handling respects privacy and labor policies.

metrics.name: avg_trust_score
metrics.description: Average perceived trustworthiness/honesty rating of the organization’s response among exposed users or raters.

metrics.name: avg_clarity_score
metrics.description: Average rating of how clearly the message explains what happened, what is unknown, and next steps.

metrics.name: willingness_to_wait_for_updates
metrics.description: Average self-reported likelihood that an audience member will wait for further updates before taking negative action (e.g., selling stock, canceling service, posting criticism).

metrics.name: misinformation_share_of_voice
metrics.description: Proportion of total relevant conversation volume dominated by the misinformation narrative vs. corrective/official narratives over the simulation window.

metrics.name: negative_sentiment_rate
metrics.description: Percentage of posts/comments classified as negative toward the brand in the monitored time window.

metrics.name: time_to_sentiment_stabilization
metrics.description: Elapsed time from misinformation onset to the point where net sentiment (e.g., positive minus negative) remains within a defined band for a sustained period.

metrics.name: corrective_message_reach
metrics.description: Number of unique users exposed to any official or partner corrective messages.

metrics.name: misinformation_reshare_rate
metrics.description: Rate at which misinformation content is reshared after the organization’s response is issued.

metrics.name: response_sla_adherence
metrics.description: Degree to which actual release times for holding statements and full updates meet predefined SLAs.
metrics.unit: percentage of responses within SLA; or minutes deviation from SLA

metrics.name: behavioral_intent_shift
metrics.description: Change in self-reported likelihood of taking adverse actions (e.g., boycotting, selling stock) before vs. after reading the response.
metrics.unit: percentage point change; or Likert scale delta

primary: avg_trust_score in the treatment group is at least 0.4 Likert units higher than in the baseline group, with statistical significance at p < 0.05 under appropriate tests.
misinformation_share_of_voice in the treatment cohort is at least 10 percentage points lower than in the baseline cohort by the end of the simulation window.
negative_sentiment_rate for treatment is at least 15% lower relative (or 5 percentage points lower absolute) than baseline in the post-response window.
secondary: willingness_to_wait_for_updates is at least 0.3 Likert units higher under treatment, indicating greater tolerance for accuracy-focused timing.
time_to_sentiment_stabilization is reduced by at least 20% under treatment compared with baseline.
behavioral_intent_shift is more favorable under treatment (e.g., smaller increase or larger decrease in intent to take adverse actions).
response_sla_adherence in treatment conditions remains within predefined organizational targets (e.g., 90% of responses within SLA), ensuring improvements do not come at unacceptable speed costs.
success_criteria.decision_rule: If primary criteria 1 and 2 are met and no critical legal/compliance breaches are identified in treatment messages, the treatment protocol should be considered for incorporation into the organization’s crisis communications playbooks, with refinement based on segment-level insights.

failure_modes.name: overly_cautious_messaging_reduces_clarity
failure_modes.description: Treatment messages might become so hedged (to satisfy legal and uncertainty constraints) that audiences perceive them as evasive, lowering trust and clarity scores.
failure_modes.detection: avg_clarity_score and avg_trust_score not significantly higher (or even lower) than baseline in Workload 2; qualitative feedback referencing vagueness or corporate-speak.

failure_modes.name: speed_cost_of_coordination
failure_modes.description: Additional coordination and legal review in treatment may delay responses beyond SLAs, amplifying narrative damage despite higher-quality content.
failure_modes.detection: response_sla_adherence significantly worse for treatment scenarios; time_to_sentiment_stabilization not improved or worsened despite better trust scores among those who see the message.

failure_modes.name: backfire_effect_in_certain_segments
failure_modes.description: Some audience segments (e.g., highly skeptical or adversarial) may interpret explicit references to AI deepfakes or verification processes as suspicious, increasing negative sentiment or belief in the misinformation.
failure_modes.detection: Segment-level analysis shows increased negative_sentiment_rate, higher misinformation_reshare_rate, or worsening behavioral_intent_shift for specific segments under treatment compared with baseline.

failure_modes.name: overreliance_on_influencers
failure_modes.description: Use of partners or influencers as amplifiers might be perceived as astroturfing or inauthentic if not chosen carefully.
failure_modes.detection: Spikes in negative sentiment specifically mentioning partners/influencers or accusing coordinated PR campaigns; narrative clusters focused on perceived manipulation rather than the core incident.

failure_modes.name: measurement_bias_and_overfitting_to_synthetic_audiences
failure_modes.description: Results may be overly optimistic or not generalize if synthetic audience behavior models are poorly calibrated to real stakeholders.
failure_modes.detection: Large discrepancies between simulated outcomes and any available historical incident data; sensitivity analysis showing results change drastically under minor parameter tweaks.

compute: Local machine or cloud notebook environment (e.g., Jupyter, VS Code) capable of running Python scripts and basic data analysis.
Optional containerized setup (e.g., Docker) with preconfigured dependencies for reproducibility.
software_dependencies: Data and scientific libraries: pandas, numpy, scipy, scikit-learn (or equivalent).
Simulation and plotting: matplotlib and/or seaborn, plotly or similar for interactive dashboards.
Optional NLP/sentiment: transformers or equivalent for model-based sentiment; or a simpler lexicon-based package.
Optional: SQLite or lightweight database driver if storing logs beyond CSV/Parquet.
data_requirements: Synthetic audience generator (provided in repository) with configurable parameters for size, segment mix, and behavioral tendencies.
Synthetic misinformation content and corresponding baseline/treatment message templates defined in structured files (JSON/YAML/Markdown).
No real PII by default; if an organization chooses to plug in internal test data, it must comply with its privacy, legal, and security policies.
governance_and_approvals: Approval from corporate communications and legal teams before adapting templates for any live or employee-facing tests.
Clear labeling and isolation of any experiments that involve real employees or customers (e.g., internal surveys) to avoid confusion with live incidents.

run_instructions: Clone the repository https://github.com/bookauthority/defending-brand-trust-ai-misinformation and navigate to the experiments/ch07_communications_under_fire/ directory (or equivalent path defined in the repo).
Set up the environment by following the provided README, typically: create and activate a virtual environment, then install dependencies (e.g., `pip install -r requirements.txt`).

Review configuration files (e.g., `config_misinformation_scenario.yml`, `config_messages.yml`, `config_simulation.yml`) to understand default parameters for scenarios, audience properties, and response SLAs.

Customize baseline and treatment messages for your organization using the provided templates, ensuring they align with your legal guidance while preserving the structural distinctions between baseline and treatment.

Run Workload 1 (social feed simulation) using the dedicated script or notebook (e.g., `01_run_social_simulation.ipynb` or `run_social_simulation.py`): this will generate synthetic engagement logs for both baseline and treatment cohorts.

Run Workload 2 (message copy A/B test) using the appropriate notebook (e.g., `02_message_ab_test.ipynb`): either use synthetic panel responses or plug in your own sandboxed survey data, keeping the experimental design consistent.

Execute Workload 3 (sentiment and narrative shift dashboard) via the analysis notebook (e.g., `03_analyze_response_impact.ipynb`): point it at the generated event logs and survey outputs to compute all defined metrics and render visualizations.

Inspect metrics and charts; compare baseline vs. treatment performance overall and by audience segment. Document findings, focusing on where treatment improves trust and narrative control and where it may introduce new risks or tradeoffs.
Adjust message templates, SLAs, and coordination rules based on insights; optionally re-run simulations with updated parameters to test revised designs.

Translate validated patterns into your operational playbooks, including checklists for message architecture, pre-approved wording, SLA matrices, and partner engagement guidelines, ensuring legal and executive sign-off.

fields.name: variant
fields.description: baseline or specific treatment variant identifier

reproducibility_notes: All random processes (e.g., user generation, behavior simulation, cohort assignment) must accept a configurable random seed stored alongside run metadata.
Each experiment run should produce a unique run_id, with configurations (parameters, seed, message file hashes) logged in a separate run_config file or table to enable exact reruns.
No outcome values should be hard-coded in the repository; notebooks and scripts should compute metrics from the logged events and ratings at run time.
